title: Maximum sum of k consecutive values
summary: Find the three consecutive days with the most library visitors, using a window that slides one day at a time.
goal: Find the k consecutive days with the most visitors

examples.label: One week, k = 3
examples.explanation: Days 2–4 (7 + 1 + 8) and days 4–6 (8 + 3 + 5) both total 16; the earlier stretch, starting on day 2, wins the tie.

examples.label: k = 1
examples.explanation: With k = 1 the busiest stretch is the single busiest day. Days 1 and 2 tie, so day 1 is reported.

examples.label: k covers every day
examples.explanation: When k equals the number of days there is only one stretch: the whole log.

ladder.name: Add up every stretch
ladder.idea: For every start day, add the k counts from scratch and keep the largest total.

ladder.name: Prefix sums
ladder.idea: Write the running total after each day once. Any stretch total is then one subtraction: `P[start + k] − P[start]`.
ladder.insight: Neighbouring stretches share almost all of their days, so the same additions are repeated. Storing running totals once removes the repetition.

ladder.name: Slide a fixed window
ladder.idea: Keep one window total. Each slide subtracts the day that leaves and adds the day that enters.
ladder.insight: Stretches are visited in order, so only the current window's total is ever needed. One running total replaces the whole prefix list.

approaches.name: Slide a fixed window
approaches.summary: Keep a running window total; each step adds the day that enters and subtracts the day that leaves.

approaches.name: Prefix sums
approaches.summary: Write running totals once, then read every stretch as the difference of two of them.

transfer.problem: A fitness tracker logs steps per hour. Find the 4-hour block with the fewest steps, to schedule a reminder to move.
transfer.explanation: It asks about every block of exactly 4 consecutive hours, so keep a fixed window of 4 and slide it, tracking the minimum instead of the maximum.

selfCheck: Adds exactly k consecutive days, never skipping one.
Keeps the earliest stretch when two totals tie.
Works for k = 1 and for k equal to the number of days.
Updates the total in constant time per step instead of re-adding k values.

aka: Maximum sum of a fixed-size window
